predecessors.name: Brythons (Celtic Britons)
predecessors.text: Cliopatria's 540 shape of Gwynedd, cut out of the sub-Roman Brythonic lands (north-west Wales and the Dee plain)

successors.name: Kingdom of England
successors.text: Gwynedd west of the Conwy (Anglesey, Caernarfonshire, Merioneth), annexed to the English Crown by the Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) and joined to the new Principality of Wales

ledger.x: 540: Gwynedd is on the map.
629: Edwin of Northumbria takes Anglesey.
633: Cadwallon wins Anglesey back by beating Edwin.
633: Cadwallon holds Northumbria.
634: Oswald defeats Cadwallon at Heavenfield and Northumbria is free.
705: the Dee plain and Vale of Clwyd pass to Mercia.

c. 825: Merfyn Frych founds the House of Aberffraw. The page: the House of Cunedda ended in the male line with Hywel ap Rhodri Molwynog c. 825; Merfyn's principal court on Anglesey gave the new dynasty its name. Same state, same colour.
855: Rhodri Mawr adds Powys.
872: Rhodri takes Seisyllwg.
878: Rhodri Mawr dies and Wales is divided among his sons: Anarawd keeps Gwynedd, Merfyn takes Powys, Cadell Deheubarth.
878: Cadell takes Seisyllwg (Deheubarth) in the division of Rhodri's lands.
942: Hywel Dda takes Gwynedd.
950: the House of Aberffraw is restored.
1039: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn becomes king of Gwynedd and Powys.
1055: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn conquers the south.
1055: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn takes Gwent.
1055: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn takes Morgannwg (he seized Morgannwg and Gwent at about the same time).
1055: Brycheiniog is inside Gruffudd's Wales.
1063: Gruffudd dies and the south is free.
1063: Gwent returns to its own line.
1063: Morgannwg returns to its own line; this page is silent on the south.
1063: Brycheiniog leaves Gruffudd's realm with the rest of the south; Cliopatria's Brycheiniog row resumes in 1066.
1063: Powys goes to the line of Bleddyn.
1063: Bleddyn and Rhiwallon ap Cynfyn, brothers of the Powys line, take Gwynedd after Gruffudd ap Llywelyn's death and agree terms with Harold.
1081: Gruffudd ap Cynan restores the Aberffraw line.
1094: the Normans hold Gwynedd.
1099: Gruffudd ap Cynan recovers Anglesey and upper Gwynedd.
1099: Cliopatria's Gwynedd shape takes one cell round Bala from its Powys shape.
1136: Owain Gwynedd takes northern Ceredigion.
1137: the brothers take the castles of central Ceredigion.
1146: Mold Castle in Tegeingl falls to Gwynedd.
1153: Rhys and Maredudd drive Hywel out of Ceredigion.
1157: after Henry II's invasion Owain cedes Tegeingl.
1169: Tegeingl is back in Gwynedd.
1208: Llywelyn annexes southern Powys and northern Ceredigion.
1210: John restores Gwenwynwyn in southern Powys.
1211: John's invasion strips Llywelyn of Tegeingl.
1212: Llywelyn recovers the Perfeddwlad.
1215: Llywelyn takes the south-west.
1216: Llywelyn the Great proclaims the Principality of Wales at the Aberdyfi council.
1216: the lesser princes of the south and west do homage to Llywelyn.
1216: Llywelyn drives Gwenwynwyn out of southern Powys again.
1234: Llywelyn holds Builth.
1240: Llywelyn the Great dies at Aberconwy Abbey on 11 April and his overlordship lapses.
1241: Dafydd submits to Henry III and gives up the lands beyond Gwynedd.
1245: Dafydd takes back Mold and Flintshire.
1247: the Treaty of Woodstock.
1256: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd crosses the Conwy.
1257: Llywelyn sweeps south.
1258: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd styles himself Prince of Wales.
1259: Dinefwr becomes a vassal kingdom of Gwynedd.
1260: Llywelyn takes Buellt.
1263: Gruffydd ap Gwenwynwyn of Powys Wenwynwyn does homage.
1267: Henry III recognises Llywelyn as Prince of Wales.
1274: Gruffydd ap Gwenwynwyn flees to England.
1277: the Treaty of Aberconwy strips Llywelyn of the Perfeddwlad.
1277: the lands that had been tributary to Llywelyn became effectively Edward's under the same treaty.
1277: Builth and the upper Wye pass to Edward with the other tributary lands.
1277: Dinefwr leaves Llywelyn's overlordship with the other tributary lands of the Treaty of Aberconwy.
1282: the last war for Gwynedd.
1283: Dolwyddelan fell in January and Dafydd was captured in June; the contest ends with the conquest.
1283: Dafydd ap Gruffudd is captured and Welsh Gwynedd ends.

wars.name: Battle of Chester
wars.outcome: Gwynedd and Powys defeated by Northumbria; 'Chester and the Cheshire Plain passed to the Anglo-Saxons'.

wars.name: Cadwallon's war on Northumbria
wars.outcome: Edwin besieged Cadwallon at Glannauc in 629; Cadwallon and Penda killed Edwin at Hatfield Chase (12 October 633) and held Northumbria for a year; Oswald killed Cadwallon at Heavenfield in 634.

wars.name: Viking and Mercian attacks on Rhodri Mawr
wars.outcome: The Dubgenti attacked Rhodri on Anglesey (Gueith Diu Sul in Mon, 877) and forced him to Ireland; he was killed by Ceolwulf of Mercia's forces in 878.

wars.name: Hywel Dda's takeover of Gwynedd
wars.outcome: After Edmund of England beat Idwal Foel, Hywel Dda took Gwynedd and Powys (942); on his death in 950 the House of Aberffraw was restored.

wars.name: Gruffydd ap Llywelyn's conquest of Wales
wars.outcome: Gruffudd killed Gruffudd ap Rhydderch (1055), took Deheubarth, Morgannwg and Gwent and ruled all Wales until 1063.

wars.name: Harold Godwinson's campaign against Gruffydd ap Llywelyn
wars.outcome: Harold struck at Rhuddlan in late 1062; in spring 1063 Tostig invaded the north and Harold's fleet the south; Gruffudd died in Snowdonia and Bleddyn and Rhiwallon were given Gwynedd and Powys.

wars.name: Norman invasion of Gwynedd
wars.outcome: Hugh of Chester's forces reached Llyn by 1090 and most of Wales was occupied by 1094; Gruffudd killed Robert of Rhuddlan at Deganwy (3 July 1093), fled to Ireland in 1098 and by 1101 Henry I recognised his claims to Anglesey, Llyn, Dunoding and Arllechwedd.

wars.name: Henry I's invasion of Gwynedd and Powys
wars.outcome: Gruffudd ap Cynan rendered homage and paid a fine but kept his lands.

wars.name: Henry II's invasions of Wales
wars.outcome: Henry's 1157 invasion ended with Owain doing homage and fealty to the King, resigning Tegeingl and Rhuddlan to Chester and restoring Cadwaladr to his Gwynedd possessions; after the 1163 revolt with Rhys ap Gruffydd Henry invaded again (1165, Owain Gwynedd…

wars.name: King John's invasion of Gwynedd
wars.outcome: John restored Gwenwynwyn to southern Powys (1210) and in 1211 invaded Gwynedd with the aid of almost all the other Welsh princes: Llywelyn lost all his lands east of the Conwy, then within two months in 1212 recovered all Gwynedd apart from the castles of…

wars.name: Llywelyn the Great's wars with the Marcher lords
wars.outcome: Hostilities with William Marshal from 1220; the Marshals retook Cardigan and Carmarthen in 1223; terms at Montgomery in October 1223 gave up his Shropshire conquests; in 1231-1234 he burnt Montgomery, New Radnor, Hay and Brecon, took Neath and Kidwelly and…

wars.name: Dafydd ap Llywelyn's wars with Henry III
wars.outcome: Gwern Eigron (August 1241) cost Dafydd his lands outside Gwynedd; he recovered Mold and Flintshire by March 1245; Henry reached the Conwy in August 1245; Dafydd died on 25 February 1246 and the Treaty of Woodstock (April 1247) cost his nephews much territory.

wars.name: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd's conquest of the Perfeddwlad and the south
wars.outcome: Bryn Derwin (June 1255), the Perfeddwlad (1256), Gwrtheyrnion and the south (1257), Buellt (January 1260), the Treaty of Pipton with Simon de Montfort (22 June 1265) and the Treaty of Montgomery (29 September 1267), which recognised him as Prince of Wales.

wars.name: Edward I's first Welsh war
wars.outcome: Edward declared war in November 1276, marched from Chester in July 1277 and Llywelyn surrendered without a major battle; the Treaty of Aberconwy (9 November 1277) left him western Gwynedd.

wars.name: Edward I's conquest of Gwynedd
wars.outcome: Dafydd's revolt, Llywelyn's death at Orewin Bridge (11 December 1282), Dolwyddelan (January 1283) and Dafydd's capture (June 1283) ended Welsh-ruled Gwynedd; the Statute of Rhuddlan followed in 1284.

certainty.note: Welsh kingdom frontiers are approximate; the one line the pages call a boundary is Offa's Dyke on the Mercian side, whose date is not given, and it is still drawn soft.
The Treaty of Montgomery (1267) and the Treaty of Aberconwy (1277) fix Llywelyn's lands by named districts, the Conwy being the line after 1277; the frontier with the Marcher lordships stays soft.

sources.title: Wales in the early Middle Ages
